transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-29 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~52 mins
Attendees: Sofia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Eli Wong (Redwood Product), Priya Nair (CTO, OrionHealth), Darren Liu (SRE Lead), Maya Singh (ML Infra), Tom Reyes (PM)

Summary (auto): quick demo of console forensics flows, emphasis on request inspector, trace playback and correlating KV cache misses to 503 spikes. Action items at end.

00:00 Sofia: Hey everyone thanks for joining, good to see the Orion team. We planned to run through the Request Forensics flow in the console, show you playback and how we correlate traces to request logs, and answer questions about retention and security. Marcus will drive the demo.
00:22 Marcus: cool, I'll share my screen, bear with me while the console loads, network's a little slow on my end. 
00:45 Marcus: Alright starting from the top, this is the Request Inspector, you can search by request id, user id, or route. I'll paste one of the sample ids Orion sent earlier - note: sample data redacted here.
01:12 Marcus: On the right we have the trace timeline, you'll see per-token latency bands, model variant, and any fallback events. Sometimes the transcription might say 'KV cash' instead of KV cache, ignore that little ocr hiccup in the auto notes.
01:40 Darren: Quick question — how granular is the trace? can we see per-layer GPU timings or is it higher level?
01:52 Marcus: It's primarily per-request and per-token timing, we show kernel phase breakdowns like attention, matmul, kv-lookup where available. We don't expose raw CUDA timings in hosted mode for multitenant customers, but Dedicated or Private with profiling enabled can surface more granular metrics.
02:20 Priya: We saw intermittent 503s in our logs last week, correlated with bursts at 3am PST. Can the Request Inspector group by time windows to find spikes?
02:35 Marcus: Yes you can aggregate by minute/hour and filter to error codes. We also surface golden metrics — e.g., sign of blocking: sudden KV cache miss rate increases. Example, here we have a cluster of requests with elevated prefix misses.
03:02 Tom: When you say 'playback' how deterministic is playback? Will it reproduce the 503 reliably?
03:12 Marcus: Good question. Playback replays the exact request payload against the same model variant pinned at that time. It tries to replicate the execution environment but if the original run used transient fallback (e.g., model ran out of capacity and fell back to a smaller model) the playback can either pin the original or emulate fallback behavior. For environment-level nondeterminism — like ephemeral infra hiccups — playback may not reproduce infra 503s 1:1; it's most useful for reproducing model-output regressions and request-level failures tied to input and kv-state.
03:50 Maya: Is there a way to replay with a fixed KV state? Our prompts use session caching heavily.
03:58 Marcus: Yes, playback has an option to include or ignore KV snapshots. You can attach the KV snapshot taken at request time; otherwise playback will run with a fresh empty prefix. That is often the key to reproducing a flakey prompt.
04:18 Eli: Also note we support partial playback where you can replay only the policy layer or the decode layer — good if you suspect a prefix caching mismatch versus tokenization differences.
04:50 Priya: On security: how are logs stored, who can access playback in the console, and how do we control that?
05:01 Sofia: For hosted customers we retain request logs according to the plan; playback is gated by RBAC in the Console — you can require SSO group membership to access playback and downloads. For Private deployments logs stay inside your VPC/S3 and KMS handles encryption, so Redwood never holds plaintext.
05:29 Darren: Do you support customer-managed KMS?
05:33 Sofia: Yes, customer-managed KMS/HSM is supported in Private and Dedicated with the appropriate entitlements. We'll attach the KMS integration guide in the follow-up.
05:50 Marcus: Back to the trace UI — here's a request that errored with a 503. You can expand the timeline to see request/response headers, upstream latency and the model's response time. The console auto-linked the nearest trace spans from our runtime.
06:18 Marcus: Note the auto-generated transcript below is imperfect — names get swapped sometimes, and acronyms like 'RBAC' get mis-typed as 'R-back' in auto notes. We try to keep the raw transcription but highlight that it's noisy.
06:40 Tom: If we run a playback and it returns 503 can you send the same trace to your infra team for root-cause?
06:47 Marcus: Absolutely. We have an internal debug escalation where we take playback artifacts + binary logs for the timeframe and can correlate scheduling and GPU OOM events if you're on Dedicated or Private. For hosted we'll surface what we can but won't expose internal cluster maps.
07:10 Priya: What's the retention policy and cost for keeping full request logs for 90 days?
07:18 Sofia: Retention is configurable; default tier stores metadata for longer but payloads are short-lived unless you opt-in. We'll send a cost estimate — generally long payload retention is billed based on GB-month and request index size.
07:34 Darren: Are there sampling options? We don't need every debug trace, just the error ones and a 5% sample of successes.
07:44 Marcus: Yep, you can configure sampling rules in the Console (by route, by status code, by user). We also support adaptive sampling — keep all errors and spike-covering samples around anomalous periods.
08:10 Maya: For the intermittent 503s, could they be caused by model switching/fallback policy?
08:17 Marcus: Definitely a candidate. If routing policy falls back under capacity pressure from a large model to a smaller one, that can cause unexpected failure modes: e.g., larger inputs buffer then hit a different kernel path which times out. The trace will show fallback events with reason codes.
08:41 Priya: Walk me through a concrete example — show us the exact steps you'd take to investigate a 503 cluster.
08:50 Marcus: Step 1: search Request Inspector for error code 503 within time window, group by route. Step 2: pick representative requests and open trace timeline -> check model variant and fallback events. Step 3: check KV cache miss rate and prefix length distributions around the spikes. Step 4: run playback with KV snapshot and pinned model variant. Step 5: if playback fails, add runtime logs and escalate.
09:20 Darren: Can Request Inspector surface correlated infra metrics like GPU utilization or queue backlog?
09:28 Marcus: For Dedicated/Private we can integrate cluster metrics and show a graph alongside traces. Hosted shows request queue lengths and latency percentiles but not host-level GPU telemetry.
09:45 Tom: You mentioned an 'Optimize' tab earlier, can it suggest batching or quantization changes to reduce these errors?
09:53 Eli: Yeah the Optimize recommendations can suggest batching windows and quant profiles given your sequence length histogram. It won't directly stop 503s, but it can reduce pressure by improving throughput and pulling down median latency.
10:15 Priya: Is there support for programmatic access to these traces? We want to pull traces into our observability pipeline.
10:22 Marcus: There's an API to stream request logs and traces into your SIEM. We typically recommend exporting to S3 + Lakehouse or hooking via Kafka for real-time.
10:36 Darren: Are you able to redact PII in logs automatically? We need PHI/PII filters.
10:44 Sofia: We have built-in redaction rules and a custom redact pipeline for Private deployments. For hosted we provide server-side redaction options and you can apply additional rules client-side before ingestion.
11:05 Tom: What's the expected timeline to set up a playback POC with our data?
11:10 Sofia: From our side, once we get sample logs and access agreed, 1-2 weeks to run a benchmark and deliver a write-up. The first step is an intake where Marcus will define the exact sample format.
11:30 Marcus: I'm going to demo the playback flow now — running a saved request id. Note: the playback console modal lets you choose 'include KV snapshot', 'pin model version' and 'use deterministic decode'.
12:05 Marcus: Starting playback... this might take a minute. The UI shows live token stream and server-side events. If it errors we'll capture debug artifacts and give you a link.
12:37 Marcus: Playback completed — in this run it returned a 200 but with longer tail latency. If this were your failing trace we'd compare to the original and check the prefix TTL and KV hit ratio.
12:56 Priya: The token stream looks different from our original capture — could it be because of sampling or tokenization differences?
13:05 Marcus: Yes, small tokenizer differences (if your client uses a different tokenizer version) can change decode boundaries. Playback defaults to the tokenizer recorded at request time but if that's missing it guesses. That can produce small output diffs.
13:30 Maya: We also use a custom text preprocessor. Will playback accept raw preprocessed input?
13:38 Marcus: You can upload the exact input payload including any preprocessor output — playback will use that verbatim. Good to include those in your sample.
13:50 Tom: Would we be able to restrict playback to an internal-only IP range? We don't want engineers outside our VPC triggering playback.
13:58 Sofia: Yes, in Private you can enforce console access only from your VPC or via VPN. Hosted has SSO/RBAC to gate playback. We'll include recommended RBAC roles in the doc.
14:20 Darren: How do audit logs record playback? We need a tamper-evident trail for compliance.
14:28 Sofia: Playback events are recorded in the audit log with user, timestamp, and the request id; audit logs can be exported to your SIEM and are signed if you use HSM-backed keys in Private.
14:50 Marcus: Switching to the error-analysis panel — here's a waterfall view showing decode phases and where the error was thrown. You can annotate spans and add comments which appear on the trace for collaboration.
15:14 Tom: Can annotations be exported to our ticketing system?
15:19 Marcus: Yep, integrations exist for JIRA, PagerDuty links can be attached. We'll show Jira mapping in the post-call docs.
15:35 Priya: For our legal team — we need to understand e-discovery implications of storing user prompts in logs. Any guidance there?
15:45 Sofia: We recommend tokenizing and hashing identifiers, storing minimal required context in metadata, and using short retention for payloads unless required. For regulated data you should use Private with your own KMS. We'll include a short legal briefing.
16:12 Maya: Regarding sampling during anomalies, does Redwood auto-increase retention in a spike window so we don't lose the critical traces?
16:20 Marcus: Our adaptive retention can keep full payloads for an hour around detected anomalies; you can tune the window and size.
16:40 Tom: We saw a note about 'request-playback synthetic load' — could you run batch synthetic replays overnight?
16:48 Marcus: Yes we offer scheduled playback runs and synthetic load tests on Dedicated instances; they can be throttled to avoid affecting production capacity.
17:05 Priya: If we start with hosted and later move to Private, can we keep playback artifacts and historical traces?
17:15 Sofia: We can migrate logs on a one-time export. If you need continuous retention across modes we'd recommend Private from the start. We'll outline migration costs in the follow-up.
17:30 Marcus: Quick demo of the trace correlation: I search for the request id, click 'correlate', it brings up related traces within +/- 2 minutes, grouped by route and user. This helps find cascading failures.
17:58 Darren: Are cascade correlations based on causality or heuristics?
18:05 Marcus: Heuristics — we use temporal and user/session correlation and shared upstream ids. We flag probable causal links but it's heuristic.
18:30 Eli: One more thing on Optimize — given Orion's seq length distribution (you shared earlier) the Optimize tab recommends lowering your max tokens and enabling 8-bit quant on medium-heavy routes to reduce memory pressure.
18:55 Priya: Would quantization affect hallucination rates?
19:01 Eli: In general lower precision can change generation quality slightly; Optimize will recommend per-route experiments and show eval diffs. We recommend A/B testing on non-critical routes first.
19:20 Tom: Ok can you show how to export a set of traces for offline analysis?
19:28 Marcus: Sure — select traces -> export -> choose S3 or webhook. The export includes a ndjson of events, token-level timings, and optional KV snapshots.
19:55 Maya: Is the download encrypted at rest during export?
20:00 Sofia: Exports to your S3 use your KMS keys if configured; if to Redwood-managed storage we encrypt with our keys but you can request customer-managed keys for Private.
20:22 Marcus: I'm going to pull an error cluster and run batch playback in the background — I'll share the job link. While that's running, any other questions?
20:35 Tom: Can we set alerting based on unusual KV miss rate?
20:40 Marcus: Yes, you can set anomaly alert rules for KV miss rate, tail latency, and error rate per route. Alerts integrate with PagerDuty or email.
20:56 Priya: For the PO C, can you include a small runbook that our oncall can follow when a 503 spike occurs?
21:03 Sofia: Absolutely — we'll include a 1-page runbook with triage steps and playbook links.
21:18 Marcus: Background job completed — I see a small set of replays that failed with a 503 reproduction for one request when KV snapshot was excluded. When I re-run with snapshot included the replay returns 200. That indicates the issue is likely cache-miss related.
21:44 Darren: That's useful — can the console surface recommended TTL adjustments or pre-warming?
21:50 Eli: Yes Optimize can suggest pre-warm strategies and cache TTL recommendations based on observed prefix reuse patterns. We'll also recommend a short-lived pre-warm for large-model routes.
22:10 Tom: Are there any differences in playback fidelity between Hosted and Dedicated?
22:16 Marcus: Dedicated playback can access more detailed infra logs and sometimes produce more deterministic replays because you can pin capacity and environment. Hosted tries to approximate but might not reproduce infra-edges like transient cluster OOM.
22:44 Maya: One of our concerns is redaction mistakes — can we run a dry-run redaction to see what's retained?
22:52 Sofia: Yes we can run a redaction simulation and produce a report showing tokens flagged. We'll add that to the security worksheet.
23:10 Priya: Let's talk about permissions — who from our team should get playback rights? We want only SRE and ML infra initially.
23:20 Sofia: Good plan. We'll propose three roles: viewer (metadata only), forensic (full playback + export), and admin. Forensic maps to SRE/ML infra.
23:40 Marcus: Quick demo of annotations and ticket creation — I'm going to flag this trace and create a JIRA ticket right from the UI. See the link pop up.
24:05 Tom: Nice. For the POC, will you need us to create a sandbox account?
24:12 Sofia: Yes, a sandbox project with representative traffic is ideal. We'll provide the ingest keys and a schema for logs.
24:30 Marcus: I'm going to show an alternate flow — using the API to stream traces into a lambda for real-time triage. This is the same payload as the console export, just streaming.
24:55 Maya: How much lag should we expect for streaming?
25:00 Marcus: Typically sub-second for logs, a few seconds for token-level events depending on network.
25:20 Priya: If we want to onboard slowly, what's the minimal footprint to get meaningful forensics?
25:28 Sofia: Start with 1% sampling on critical routes + full error retention for 7 days. That usually surfaces most problems and keeps cost low.
25:45 Darren: Can you show cost ballpark for that config?
25:50 Sofia: We'll send a tailored estimate but rough math: ingest size x retention days x compression. I'll add a sample calc for the 1% plan.
26:10 Marcus: Demo note: sometimes the auto-transcribe splits speakers incorrectly; you'll see Speaker 2 and Speaker 3 in the raw export. We recommend using the timestamps as the authoritative sequence.
26:35 Tom: A couple smaller questions — do you have an oncall runbook template?
26:41 Sofia: Yes, included in post-call materials.
26:50 Eli: For the POC scope, we'll propose: 1) ingest 24h logs, 2) run 48h playback benchmark, 3) produce triage report with recommended config changes.
27:05 Priya: Sounds good. Can we lock the POC to not affect production quotas?
27:12 Marcus: Yes, we can provision a sandbox Dedicated slice or throttle hosted runs to ensure no impact.
27:30 Tom: Any gotchas we should watch for when exporting logs?
27:35 Marcus: Ensure timestamps are in UTC, include the model variant and prefixes, and if you rely on KV, include snapshots. Missing fields make reproducing harder.
27:54 Darren: Do you have an SLA for playback jobs?
27:58 Marcus: No formal SLA for playback in hosted but Dedicated customers can get faster turnaround under contract. We aim for same-day triage during POC windows.
28:18 Priya: Ok let's recap the next steps.
28:22 Sofia: Recap: Sofia sends security pack and RBAC mapping; Marcus shares playback sample format; Orion provides 24h logs and 3 failing traces; schedule POC scoping call for 2025-12-10.
28:40 Tom: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
28:44 Priya: Thanks — appreciate the clear path. We'll get the logs over and coordinate legal on the KMS question.
29:00 Sofia: Thanks all. We'll follow up with the doc bundle and a calendar invite for the scoping meeting.

End of transcript (partial automated timestamps every ~30-60s).
questions: How does KV snapshot inclusion change replay fidelity?
What RBAC controls exist for playback and export?
Can we auto-redact PII/PHI in logs before storage?
